<!-- problem-1: body_md -->
\label{q:hengartner}
{\it Let $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ be complex-valued pluriharmonic functions on the unit
ball $B\subset\mathbb C^n$, and put $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$.  Is $F$ locally univalent
if and only if its real Jacobian does not vanish?}
<!-- end problem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:phase-criterion}
Let $q\colon(\mathbb C^n,0)\to(\mathbb C,0)$ be a nonconstant holomorphic germ, $n\ge1$.
For $\theta\in\mathbb R$, set
\[
   X_\theta(q):=\{z:\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}q(z))=0\}.
\]
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $dq(0)\ne0$;
\item for every $\theta\in\mathbb R$, the germ $X_\theta(q)$ is a smooth
      real-analytic hypersurface at $0$;
\item for some $\theta\in\mathbb R$, the local rational homology of $X_\theta(q)$
      at $0$ is that of $\mathbb R^{2n-1}$, namely
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-Q-homology}
H_j\bigl(X_\theta(q),X_\theta(q)\setminus\{0\};\mathbb Q\bigr)
 \cong
 \begin{cases}
   \mathbb Q,&j=2n-1,\\
   0,&j\ne2n-1.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Thus, at a holomorphic critical point, no phase hypersurface $X_\theta(q)$ is
even a rational homology manifold of the expected dimension.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:lewy}
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$ be a domain, $n\ge1$, and let
$F\colon\Omega\to\mathbb C^n$ be pluriharmonic.  For every $p\in\Omega$, the
following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $F$ is one-to-one on a neighborhood of $p$;
\item $J_{\!\mathbb R} F(p)\ne0$;
\item $F$ is a local real-analytic diffeomorphism at $p$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, Hengartner's Problem~3.10(a) has an affirmative answer in every
complex dimension.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:bilipschitz-intro}
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n\cong\mathbb R^{2n}$ be a bounded domain with $C^1$-Dini
boundary.  Every quasiconformal pluriharmonic homeomorphism
\[
      F\colon\mathbb B^n\longrightarrow\Omega
\]
is bi-Lipschitz.  In particular, every quasiconformal pluriharmonic
self-homeomorphism of $\mathbb B^n$ is bi-Lipschitz.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:primitive}
Let $U\subset\mathbb C^n$ be a ball and let $u\in C^2(U,\mathbb R)$ be pluriharmonic.  Then
there is a holomorphic function $q$ on $U$ such that $u=\operatorname{Re} q$.  The
function $q$ is unique up to an imaginary constant.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The $(1,0)$-form
\[
       \alpha:=2\partial u
       =2\sum_{j=1}^n u_{z_j}\,dz_j
\]
has holomorphic coefficients because $\overline\partial\partial u=0$, and it
is $\partial$-closed.  The holomorphic Poincar\'e lemma on the ball gives a
holomorphic function $q$ with $dq=\alpha$.  Since
\[
       d(\operatorname{Re} q)=\operatorname{Re}(dq)=\operatorname{Re}(2\partial u)=du,
\]
$u-\operatorname{Re} q$ is constant; changing the real part of the additive constant in
$q$ gives the identity.  If two holomorphic functions have the same real
part, their difference is a purely imaginary constant.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:real-complex}
Let $q$ be holomorphic near $p\in\mathbb C^n$.  Then
\[
       d(\operatorname{Re} q)_p=0\Longleftrightarrow dq_p=0.
\]
More precisely, in standard coordinates,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gradient-identity}
   |\nabla \operatorname{Re} q|^2=\sum_{j=1}^n\left|\frac{\partial q}{\partial z_j}\right|^2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Write $q=u+iv$.  The Cauchy--Riemann equations in each variable give
\[
   q_{z_j}=u_{x_j}-iu_{y_j},
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:gradient-identity} and hence the equivalence.  One may
also argue invariantly: if $d(\operatorname{Re} q)_p(v)=0$ for every real tangent vector
$v$, then applying the same identity to $iv$ shows that both the real and the
imaginary parts of $dq_p(v)$ vanish.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:reduction}
Let $F\colon\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$ be pluriharmonic and suppose that $F$
is one-to-one on a neighborhood of $p\in\Omega$.  If $J_{\!\mathbb R} F(p)=0$, then there
exist a nonzero real linear functional $\ell\colon\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb R$, a ball
$U\ni p$, and a nonconstant holomorphic function $q$ on $U$ such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $q(p)=0$ and $dq(p)=0$;
\item $\{\operatorname{Re} q=0\}=F^{-1}(F(U)\cap H)$ in $U$, where
\[
       H:=\{w:\ell(w)=\ell(F(p))\};
\]
\item the germ of the ambient pair
\[
   \bigl(U,\{\operatorname{Re} q=0\}\bigr)
\]
at $p$ is homeomorphic to the germ of
$\bigl(\mathbb R^{2n},\mathbb R^{2n-1}\bigr)$ at the origin.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, $\{\operatorname{Re} q=0\}$ has the local rational and integral homology
of $\mathbb R^{2n-1}$ at $p$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Shrink to an open ball $U$ on which $F$ is injective.  Since the real linear
map $dF_p\colon\mathbb R^{2n}\to\mathbb R^{2n}$ is singular, there is a nonzero real
covector $\ell$ such that $\ell\circ dF_p=0$.  Set
\[
       u(z):=\ell(F(z))-\ell(F(p)).
\]
Every real linear combination of the real coordinate functions of $F$ is
real-valued pluriharmonic, so $u$ is pluriharmonic and $du(p)=0$.

The function $u$ is not constant.  Indeed, invariance of domain implies that
$F(U)$ is open in $\mathbb R^{2n}$; if $u$ were constant, $F(U)$ would be contained
in the affine hyperplane $H$, which has empty interior.  After shrinking $U$
if needed, Lemma~\ref{lem:primitive} gives a nonconstant holomorphic $q$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re} q$ and $q(p)=0$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:real-complex}, $dq(p)=0$.

Again by invariance of domain, $F\colon U\to F(U)$ is a homeomorphism onto an
open set.  Moreover,
\[
   \{z\in U:\operatorname{Re} q(z)=0\}
      =F^{-1}(F(U)\cap H).
\]
Thus $F$ is a homeomorphism of pairs
\[
 \bigl(U,\{\operatorname{Re} q=0\}\bigr)
   \longrightarrow
 \bigl(F(U),F(U)\cap H\bigr).
\]
Since $F(U)$ is a neighborhood of $F(p)$ and $H$ is an affine hyperplane
through $F(p)$, the last pair is the standard locally flat hyperplane pair.
The local-homology assertion follows.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:local-link}
For every sufficiently small admissible $\varepsilon$ and every integer $j$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-link}
 H_j(X,X\setminus\{0\};\mathbb Q)
   \cong \widetilde H_{j-1}\bigl(L_\varepsilon(X);\mathbb Q\bigr).
\end{equation}
Here the left-hand side is computed in a sufficiently small representative of
the germ.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
By local conical structure, the relevant pair is homeomorphic to
$(CL,CL\setminus\{v\})$, where $L=L_\varepsilon(X)$ and $v$ is the cone
point.  The cone is contractible and its punctured cone deformation retracts
onto $L$.  The long exact sequence of the pair gives
\[
 H_j(CL,CL\setminus\{v\};\mathbb Q)
    \cong \widetilde H_{j-1}(L;\mathbb Q).
\]
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:homology-link}
If $X$ has at $0$ the local rational homology of $\mathbb R^d$, then every
sufficiently small admissible link of $X$ has the rational homology of
$S^{d-1}$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
This is immediate from Lemma~\ref{lem:local-link}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:alexander}
Let $L\subset S^m$, $m\ge1$, be a compact locally contractible subset having
the rational homology of $S^{m-1}$.  Then $S^m\setminus L$ has exactly two
connected components, and each component is rationally acyclic.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Alexander duality over $\mathbb Q$ gives, for every $i$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:alexander}
  \widetilde H_i(S^m\setminus L;\mathbb Q)
       \cong \widetilde H^{m-i-1}(L;\mathbb Q);
\end{equation}
see \cite{Bredon1993,Hatcher2002}.  The universal coefficient theorem and the
homology assumption show that the right-hand side is $\mathbb Q$ for $i=0$ and zero
for $i>0$.  Since the complement is an open subset of a manifold, it is
locally path connected.  Hence $\widetilde H_0(S^m\setminus L;\mathbb Q)\cong\mathbb Q$ says that
the complement has exactly two components, say $V_1,V_2$.  For $i>0$,
\[
 H_i(S^m\setminus L;\mathbb Q)
    \cong H_i(V_1;\mathbb Q)\oplus H_i(V_2;\mathbb Q)=0.
\]
Each $V_k$ is connected, so its reduced $H_0$ also vanishes.  Thus both
components are rationally acyclic.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:no-schoenflies}
No generalized Schoenflies theorem is used.  The link need not be an unknotted
sphere, or even a topological manifold.  Its rational homology and Alexander
duality already give exactly the information required below.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:acampo}
Let $q\colon(\mathbb C^n,0)\to(\mathbb C,0)$ be holomorphic.  If
$q\in\mathfrak m_{\mathbb C^n,0}^{,2}$, equivalently $q(0)=0$ and $dq(0)=0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:acampo-zero}
       \Lambda(h_q)=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:acyclic-lefschetz}
If $P$ is a nonempty connected space of finite homological type and
$\widetilde H_j(P;\mathbb Q)=0$ for all $j\ge0$, then every self-homeomorphism
$h\colon P\to P$ satisfies
\(
       \Lambda(h)=1.
\)
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The only nonzero rational homology group is $H_0(P;\mathbb Q)\cong\mathbb Q$.  Every
self-map of a connected space induces the identity on $H_0$, so its Lefschetz
number is $1$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:sign-fiber}
For $\theta\in\mathbb R$, let
\[
 U_{\theta,+}:=
 \{z\in S_\varepsilon^{2n-1}:\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}q(z))>0\}.
\]
If
\[
 I_{\theta,+}:=
 \{e^{it}\in S^1:\theta-\tfrac\pi2<t<\theta+\tfrac\pi2\},
\]
then
\[
       U_{\theta,+}=\Phi_q^{-1}(I_{\theta,+}).
\]
Consequently, $U_{\theta,+}\simeq P_q$.  The analogous statement holds for
the negative sign region.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
For $z\notin K_q$,
\[
 \operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}q(z))>0
\Longleftrightarrow
 \operatorname{Re}\!\left(e^{-i\theta}\frac{q(z)}{|q(z)|}\right)>0,
\]
which is equivalent to $\Phi_q(z)\in I_{\theta,+}$.  The restriction of the
fiber bundle \eqref{eq:spherical-milnor} to the contractible open semicircle
$I_{\theta,+}$ is fiber-homotopy trivial (indeed smoothly trivial), so its
total space is homotopy equivalent to $P_q$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The implication (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:real-complex} applied to $e^{-i\theta}q$: if $dq(0)\ne0$, then
$d\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}q)_0\ne0$ for every $\theta$, and the real-analytic
implicit function theorem gives a smooth hypersurface.  The implication
(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii) is immediate.

It remains to prove (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i).  Suppose that
\eqref{eq:local-Q-homology} holds for a phase $\theta$ and assume, toward a
contradiction, that $dq(0)=0$.  Multiplication by $e^{-i\theta}$ does not
change criticality or monodromy, so we may replace $q$ by
$e^{-i\theta}q$ and assume $\theta=0$.  Put
\[
       X:=\{\operatorname{Re} q=0\}.
\]

Choose $\varepsilon>0$ sufficiently small so that the local conical structure
of $X$, the local-homology link description, and the Milnor fibration all hold
on $S_\varepsilon^{2n-1}$.  Such radii form a cofinal set at the origin by the
subanalytic conical structure theorem and Milnor's fibration theorem.  Let
\[
       L:=X\cap S_\varepsilon^{2n-1}.
\]
By Corollary~\ref{cor:homology-link}, $L$ has the rational homology of
$S^{2n-2}$.  The link is compact and semianalytic, hence triangulable and
locally contractible.  Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:alexander} in
$S_\varepsilon^{2n-1}$, we conclude that its complement has exactly two
connected components and that each is rationally acyclic.

The complement is the disjoint union
\[
 S_\varepsilon^{2n-1}\setminus L=U_+\sqcup U_-,
 \quad
 U_\pm:=\{z\in S_\varepsilon^{2n-1}:\pm\operatorname{Re} q(z)>0\}.
\]
Both sign regions are nonempty.  Indeed, $u=\operatorname{Re} q$ is a nonconstant real
harmonic function with $u(0)=0$.  If $u\ge0$ on the sphere, the minimum
principle first gives $u\ge0$ in the ball and then, from the interior minimum
$u(0)=0$, forces $u$ to be constant.  The same argument applied to $-u$
excludes $u\le0$ on the sphere.

Because the complement has exactly two components, and $U_+$ and $U_-$ are
disjoint nonempty open subsets whose union is the complement, each $U_\pm$ is
one full component.  Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sign-acyclic}
       \widetilde H_j(U_+;\mathbb Q)=0\quad(j\ge0).
\end{equation}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:sign-fiber}, $U_+\simeq P_q$, so $P_q$ is nonempty, connected,
and rationally acyclic.  Thus Lemma~\ref{lem:acyclic-lefschetz} gives
\[
       \Lambda(h_q)=1.
\]
On the other hand, $q(0)=0$ and $dq(0)=0$, so $q\in\mathfrak m^2$ and A'Campo's
theorem gives $\Lambda(h_q)=0$.  This contradiction proves $dq(0)\ne0$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:formulations}
For a nonconstant holomorphic germ $q\colon(\mathbb C^n,0)\to(\mathbb C,0)$, the following
are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $dq(0)\ne0$;
\item $\{\operatorname{Re} q=0\}$ is a smooth real-analytic hypersurface germ at $0$;
\item $\{\operatorname{Re} q=0\}$ is a topological $(2n-1)$-manifold germ at $0$;
\item $\{\operatorname{Re} q=0\}$ is a rational homology $(2n-1)$-manifold at $0$.
\end{enumerate}
If these conditions hold, the hypersurface is locally flat in $\mathbb R^{2n}$; if
$dq(0)=0$, it is not even a rational homology manifold at $0$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The implications
$\textup{(i)}\Rightarrow\textup{(ii)}\Rightarrow
 \textup{(iii)}\Rightarrow\textup{(iv)}$
are standard, while $\textup{(iv)}\Rightarrow\textup{(i)}$ is
\cref{thm:phase-criterion}.  A smooth hypersurface is locally flat by the
implicit function theorem.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:every-phase}
If $dq(0)=0$, then for every real line $L\subset\mathbb C$ through $0$, the inverse
image germ $q^{-1}(L)$ fails to be a rational homology $(2n-1)$-manifold at
$0$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Every real line through $0$ is
$e^{i(\theta+\pi/2)}\mathbb R$, and its inverse image is
$X_\theta(q)$.  Apply \cref{thm:phase-criterion}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:quadratic}
For
\[
       q(z)=z_1^2+\cdots+z_n^2,
       \quad z=x+iy,
\]
one has $\operatorname{Re} q=|x|^2-|y|^2$.  Hence the link of
$\{\operatorname{Re} q=0\}$ on $S_\varepsilon^{2n-1}$ is
\[
 S^{n-1}_{\varepsilon/\sqrt2}\times
 S^{n-1}_{\varepsilon/\sqrt2}.
\]
For $n\ge2$ this has nontrivial middle homology and is not a homology
$S^{2n-2}$; for $n=1$ it consists of four points rather than two.  This model
exhibits concretely the homology detected by the proof.  The general argument
shows that some homological obstruction persists for every critical
holomorphic germ, even when its critical locus is nonisolated or its zero
divisor is nonreduced.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The implication (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii) is the real inverse function theorem;
pluriharmonic mappings are real analytic.  The implication
(iii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is immediate.

For (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii), assume that $F$ is injective near $p$ and suppose
that $J_{\!\mathbb R} F(p)=0$.  By Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction}, there is a nonconstant
holomorphic $q$ near $p$ such that $dq(p)=0$ while
$\{\operatorname{Re} q=0\}$ is a locally flat hypersurface germ.  After translating
$p$ to $0$, this contradicts Corollary~\ref{cor:formulations}.  Therefore
$J_{\!\mathbb R} F(p)\ne0$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:branch-identity}
For every pluriharmonic map $F\colon\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:branch-identity}
       \mathcal B_{\mathrm{inj}}(F)
       =\operatorname{Crit}_{\mathbb R}(F):=\{p\in\Omega:J_{\!\mathbb R} F(p)=0\}.
\end{equation}
In particular, the local univalence locus is precisely the regular locus of
$F$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:lewy}, a locally injective point is regular, which gives
$\operatorname{Crit}_{\mathbb R}(F)\subset\mathcal B_{\mathrm{inj}}(F)$.  Conversely, the inverse
function theorem makes $F$ locally injective at every point where
$J_{\!\mathbb R} F\ne0$.  Taking the contrapositive gives the reverse inclusion.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:dichotomy}
Assume that $\Omega$ is connected.  Exactly one of the following occurs:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $J_{\!\mathbb R} F\equiv0$, and $F$ is locally injective nowhere;
\item $\mathcal B_{\mathrm{inj}}(F)$ is a proper closed real-analytic subset
of $\Omega$ of real dimension at most $2n-1$, hence has empty interior and
$2n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.  On its open dense complement, $F$ is
a local real-analytic diffeomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
If $J_{\!\mathbb R} F\equiv0$, the first alternative follows from
Theorem~\ref{thm:branch-identity}.  Otherwise the zero set of the nontrivial real
analytic function $J_{\!\mathbb R} F$ is a proper real-analytic subset of codimension at
least one, and therefore has empty interior and measure zero; see, for example,
\cite{KrantzParks2002}.  Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:branch-identity} again.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:global-diffeo}
If $F\colon\Omega\to\mathbb C^n$ is injective and pluriharmonic, then
$J_{\!\mathbb R} F$ is nowhere zero and $F$ is a real-analytic diffeomorphism from
$\Omega$ onto the open set $F(\Omega)$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:lewy} at every point.  Invariance of domain makes $F(\Omega)$
open and $F$ a homeomorphism onto its image.  The local real-analytic inverses
given by the inverse function theorem agree with the global inverse.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:orientation}
If $\Omega$ is connected and
$F\colon\Omega\to F(\Omega)\subset\mathbb C^n$ is a pluriharmonic homeomorphism,
then $J_{\!\mathbb R} F$ has a constant nonzero sign on $\Omega$.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By Corollary~\ref{cor:global-diffeo}, $J_{\!\mathbb R} F$ is continuous and nowhere zero.  Its
sign is constant on the connected domain $\Omega$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
View $\mathbb B^n$ and $\Omega$ as domains in $\mathbb R^{2n}$.  Since $F$ is a
homeomorphism, it is locally injective.  Theorem~\ref{thm:lewy} gives
\[
       J_{\!\mathbb R} F(z)\ne0\quad(z\in\mathbb B^n),
\]
so $F$ is a local real-analytic, hence local $C^1$, diffeomorphism.  Each real
coordinate of a pluriharmonic mapping is harmonic.  Kalaj's theorem therefore
applies with $m=2n$ and yields the bi-Lipschitz conclusion.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:distortion}
For general harmonic quasiconformal mappings in $\mathbb R^m$, pointwise Jacobian
nondegeneracy is not automatic.  A known sufficient condition is the
small-distortion bound $K_O<3^{m-1}$
\cite{BozinMateljevic2015}; see also \cite{AstalaManojlovic2015} for related
higher-dimensional extensions of Pavlovi\'c-type regularity.  In the
pluriharmonic class, Theorem~\ref{thm:lewy} supplies nondegeneracy with no smallness
condition on the quasiconformal distortion.  Thus
Corollary~\ref{cor:bilipschitz-intro} extends the complex two-dimensional conclusion
in \cite[Corollary~24]{Kalaj2026} to every $n\ge1$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
